About this evidence

What these findings do—and do not—show

480 myths from 45 completed runs, balanced by design across September/frontier cohorts, task orders, group sizes and mixing. The 44 events are selected examples, not a census or prevalence estimate. Semantic labels are inherited exploratory machine readings; human reliability remains unestablished.

Textual borrowing, borrowing of advice, and changing behavior are separate claims. Actual exposure has 1.08 percentage points more novel five-word overlap than matched unseen text (run SD 2.61; descriptive run-bootstrap interval 0.43–1.89). This is lexical, not causal or semantic evidence.

The behavioral window ends before the next own myth. Conditional tests require measurable triggers, not an invented definition of “poor” or “a season.” Only two of six explicit-amount cases have a clean immediate sender opportunity; both already sent that amount. Insufficient evidence is not a null effect.

Source comparison quotes are exact excerpts. Highlights locate them in complete stories; absence of a highlight can mean no supporting quote was selected. “Previous own” is the immediately preceding myth; the selected earlier comparison can be older. A matched unseen myth comes from another run, not an interaction partner.
